```{r}
#| label: setup
source("functions.R")
pop <- populations$exponential
```

# 1. What population are you sampling from?

The exponential distribution with rate 1 models a waiting time, such as the time until the next customer arrives.
Its mean and standard deviation are both 1. It is strongly right skewed (skewness 2), has a heavier right tail than a
normal distribution (excess kurtosis 6), and can never be negative. This is the population where I expected the
"n = 30" rule to be tested hardest among the iid populations with finite variance.

To see how different this population is from the normal one I used as my control in 01normal.qmd, I drew both
side by side. On the exponential panel I also drew a normal curve with the same mean and standard deviation (both 1).

```{r}
#| label: population
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4.5
set.seed(student_id)
normalDraws <- populations$normal$generator(100000)
set.seed(student_id)
popDraws <- pop$generator(100000)

old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
hist(normalDraws, breaks = 60, probability = TRUE, col = "gray85", border = "white", xlim = c(-4, 4),
     main = "Normal(0, 1) population (01normal)", xlab = "Individual value")
curve(dnorm(x), add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)

hist(popDraws, breaks = 80, probability = TRUE, col = "gray85", border = "white", xlim = c(-2, 6),
     main = "Exponential(1) population", xlab = "Individual value")
curve(dexp(x, rate = 1), from = 0, add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
curve(dnorm(x, mean = 1, sd = 1), add = TRUE, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Exponential(1) density", "Normal with mean 1, SD 1"),
       col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"), lwd = 2, lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
par(old)

data.frame(
  quantity    = c("mean", "sd", "skewness", "excess kurtosis"),
  theoretical = c(pop$mu, pop$sigma, pop$gamma1, pop$gamma2),
  simulated   = c(mean(popDraws), sd(popDraws), skewness(popDraws), exKurtosis(popDraws))
)
```

The simulated values are close to the theoretical ones. Skewness and kurtosis are a little further off than the mean
and SD, which makes sense: they depend on the rare large values in the right tail.

The two populations on the right panel have the same mean and the same standard deviation, but very different shapes.
The normal curve puts about `r round(100 * pnorm(0, mean = 1, sd = 1), 1)` percent of its values below 0, where the exponential has none, and
the exponential has a long right tail that the normal curve does not. Since the CLT formula sigma / sqrt(n) only
uses the mean and SD, it cannot see this difference; only the shape of the sampling distribution can.

# 2. What did you expect before running the simulation?

## The exponential formula

The exponential distribution with rate lambda has density

$$f(x) = \lambda e^{-\lambda x}, \qquad x \ge 0,$$

with mean 1 / lambda, standard deviation 1 / lambda, skewness 2 and excess kurtosis 6. The density is highest at
x = 0 and keeps falling as x grows. Lambda only sets the time scale: the skewness and kurtosis do not depend on it.
To check this with numbers, I plugged lambda = 1, 10 and 100 into the formula and also simulated 100,000 values from each.

```{r}
#| label: lambdaPlot
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 3.8
lambdas <- c(1, 10, 100)
lamDraws <- lapply(lambdas, function(l) {
  set.seed(student_id)
  rexp(100000, rate = l)
})
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, length(lambdas)), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
for (i in 1:length(lambdas)) {
  l <- lambdas[i]
  hist(lamDraws[[i]][lamDraws[[i]] < 6 / l], breaks = 60, probability = TRUE, col = "gray85", border = "white",
       xlim = c(0, 6 / l), main = paste("lambda =", l), xlab = "x")
  curve(l * exp(-l * x), from = 0, to = 6 / l, n = 500, add = TRUE, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2)
}
par(old)

data.frame(
  lambda = lambdas,
  mean = sapply(lamDraws, mean),
  theoMean = 1 / lambdas,
  sd = sapply(lamDraws, sd),
  skewness = sapply(lamDraws, skewness),
  exKurtosis = sapply(lamDraws, exKurtosis)
)
```

The three panels look the same; only the numbers on the x axis change. The mean and SD shrink as 1 / lambda, but the
simulated skewness and kurtosis are identical for all three. They match exactly because, with the same seed, R makes
the draws for rate lambda by dividing the draws for rate 1 by lambda, and dividing by a constant does not change shape. So my results for lambda = 1 apply to every exponential
population, the same way the results for N(0, 1) applied to every normal population in 01normal.qmd.

## The right tail

The skewness of 2 comes from the long right tail. To see how long it is, I compared the chance of a value larger
than x for the exponential and for a normal distribution with the same mean and SD (both 1).

```{r}
#| label: tailCompare
x <- 1:6
tailCompare <- data.frame(
  x = x,
  exponential = 1 - pexp(x, rate = 1),
  normal = 1 - pnorm(x, mean = 1, sd = 1)
)
tailCompare$ratio <- tailCompare$exponential / tailCompare$normal
knitr::kable(signif(tailCompare, 3))
```

Up to x = 2 the two are similar, but beyond that the ratio grows very fast: the exponential is about
`r round(tailCompare$ratio[x == 4])` times more likely than the normal to give a value above 4, and about
`r format(round(tailCompare$ratio[x == 6]), big.mark = ",")` times more likely above 6. These rare large values pull a sample mean to the right, and a
handful of them can do it even when n is moderate. That is why I expected the sample mean to stay right skewed
for a long time.

## My predictions

I made four predictions before running anything.

Center and spread: the mean of the sample means should be mu = 1 and their SD should be sigma / sqrt(n) = 1 / sqrt(n)
at every n, including n = 1. These two results only need independence and a finite variance, not normality, so I
did not expect the SE check to fail anywhere.

Shape at small n: the sampling distribution should start out right skewed like the population, with a short left
tail and a long right tail, and the QQ plot should bend upward at both ends.

How fast the shape improves: for iid data the skewness of the sample mean is gamma1 / sqrt(n) = 2 / sqrt(n) and the
excess kurtosis is gamma2 / n = 6 / n. My skewness cutoff is `r criteria$skew`, so the formula predicts I need

```{r}
#| label: prediction
predictedN(pop$gamma1)
iidPrediction(pop$gamma1, pop$gamma2)(30)
```

The kurtosis cutoff (`r criteria$kurt`) only needs 6 / n ≤ `r criteria$kurt`, which is n ≥ `r ceiling(pop$gamma2 / criteria$kurt)`, so I expected
skewness to be the check that decides the answer. At the rule of thumb n = 30 the predicted skewness is still
`r round(2 / sqrt(30), 3)`, almost twice my cutoff, so I expected n = 30 not to be enough. There is no simple formula for
the QQ correlation, so that check I had to measure.

Shapiro Wilk: with 5,000 values per test, I expected it to reject normality at almost every n, even after my
own checks pass, because a test that large detects very small departures.

# 3. Which sample sizes did you investigate?

## Coarse grid, then a finer grid

I started with a coarse grid: `r paste(pop$coarse, collapse = ", ")`. The values are spread out on a roughly log scale
because the prediction (n near `r predictedN(pop$gamma1)`) is far from the small n values. After the coarse grid, my code finds
the last n that failed and the first n that passed, and adds about 12 values between them.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
res <- analyzePopulation(pop)
tab <- res$table
nStar <- smallestN(tab)
added <- setdiff(tab$n, pop$coarse)
showTable(tab)
```

The finer grid added `r paste(added, collapse = ", ")`.

## Choosing my QQ cutoff

On the normal population every QQ cutoff up to 0.9995 passed, so the normal file could not tell me which QQ cutoff
to use. Here the QQ check matters, so I compared three values, keeping the skewness and kurtosis cutoffs the same.

```{r}
#| label: qqCompare
qqValues <- c(0.995, 0.998, 0.999)
qqCompare <- data.frame(
  qqCut = qqValues,
  chosenN = sapply(qqValues, function(q) {
    crit <- criteria
    crit$qqCor <- q
    smallestN(tab, crit)
  })
)
knitr::kable(qqCompare)
row100 <- tab[tab$n == 100, ]
```

With 0.995 and 0.998 the answer is the same as with skewness alone, so the QQ check agrees with the skewness check.
With 0.999 the answer moves to `r qqCompare$chosenN[qqValues == 0.999]`: at n = 100 the skewness was already
`r round(row100$skew, 3)`, below my cutoff, but the QQ correlation was `r round(row100$qqCor, 4)`. A cutoff of 0.999 would
let the QQ check overrule the skewness check on its own, so I kept 0.998, which keeps the two checks consistent.

## How much does the answer depend on my skewness cutoff?

My answer depends on my definition of "normal enough". To see how much, I ran a wider grid once and found the
smallest n for several skewness cutoffs, keeping the other cutoffs the same.

```{r}
#| label: skewCompare
wideGrid <- c(5, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 300, 400, 500, 700, 1000)
wide <- runGrid(pop$generator, wideGrid, pop$mu,
                theoSE = iidSE(pop$sigma), pred = iidPrediction(pop$gamma1, pop$gamma2))
skewValues <- c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5)
skewCompare <- data.frame(
  skewCut = skewValues,
  predictedN = sapply(skewValues, function(s) predictedN(pop$gamma1, s)),
  chosenN = sapply(skewValues, function(s) {
    crit <- criteria
    crit$skew <- s
    smallestN(wide$table, crit)
  })
)
knitr::kable(skewCompare)
```

Halving the skewness cutoff from 0.2 to 0.1 multiplies the required n by about 4, as the formula (2 / cutoff)² says.
For looser cutoffs (0.3 and 0.5) the answer stops following the skewness formula, because the QQ check becomes the
one that decides. So there is no single "right" n for this population: the answer is only meaningful together with
the standard used to define "normal enough".

# 4. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = `r nStar`}$$

```{r}
#| label: summaryNumbers
star     <- tab[tab$n == nStar, ]
lastFail <- tab[tab$n == max(tab$n[tab$n < nStar & !tab$normalEnough]), ]
failed   <- c(skewness = abs(lastFail$skew) > criteria$skew,
              kurtosis = abs(lastFail$exKurt) > criteria$kurt,
              QQ = lastFail$qqCor < criteria$qqCor)
at30     <- tab[tab$n == 30, ]
lucky    <- tab$n[tab$n < nStar & tab$normalEnough]
seRange  <- range(tab$seRatio)
meanGapZ <- abs(tab$simMean - tab$theoMean) / (tab$theoSE / sqrt(num))
```

The prediction from section 2 was n = `r predictedN(pop$gamma1)`, and the simulation gave n = `r nStar`. The plot below shows
why. Skewness was the check that decided the answer, so it shows the skewness of the sample means for every n I
tested between 50 and 200.

```{r}
#| label: whyN
#| fig.width: 10
#| fig.height: 5.5
zoom <- tab[tab$n >= 50 & tab$n <= 200, ]
nLine <- seq(50, 200, length.out = 300)
band <- 1.96 * sqrt(6 / num)
plot(NULL, xlim = c(50, 200), ylim = c(0.05, 0.35),
     xlab = "Sample size n", ylab = "Skewness of the sample means",
     main = paste0("Why n = ", nStar, ": skewness near the cutoff"))
polygon(c(nLine, rev(nLine)), c(2 / sqrt(nLine) + band, rev(2 / sqrt(nLine) - band)),
        col = "gray90", border = NA)
lines(nLine, 2 / sqrt(nLine), col = "black", lwd = 2)
abline(h = criteria$skew, col = "firebrick", lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(v = nStar, col = "steelblue", lwd = 2, lty = 3)
points(zoom$n, zoom$skew, pch = ifelse(zoom$normalEnough, 16, 4), cex = 1.4,
       col = ifelse(zoom$normalEnough, "steelblue", "firebrick"), lwd = 2)
legend("topright",
       c("Prediction 2 / sqrt(n)", "Monte Carlo noise band (95%)", paste("Cutoff", criteria$skew),
         paste("Chosen n =", nStar), "Passed all checks", "Failed a check"),
       col = c("black", "gray80", "firebrick", "steelblue", "steelblue", "firebrick"),
       lty = c(1, NA, 2, 3, NA, NA), lwd = c(2, NA, 2, 2, 2, 2), pch = c(NA, 15, NA, NA, 16, 4),
       pt.cex = c(NA, 2, NA, NA, 1.4, 1.4), bty = "n")
```

How to read it: the black line is the skewness the formula predicts, and the gray band is roughly how far the simulated value can move by Monte Carlo noise alone (about ±`r round(band, 3)`, using the noise formula sqrt(6 / num) from 01normal.qmd, which is a rough guide for a skewed population). The predicted line crosses my cutoff (red dashed) exactly at n = `r predictedN(pop$gamma1)`. To the left of that point the true skewness is above the cutoff, so a point
can only fall below it by luck: that is what happened at n = `r paste(lucky, collapse = " and ")` (blue dots on the left),
and the n values right after them failed again. From n = `r nStar` on, every point passed, so `r nStar` is the smallest n
that I can defend. Because the line crosses the cutoff right at 100, a different seed could move the answer by a
few n in either direction.

# 5. How do the simulated mean and standard error compare with theory?

```{r}
#| label: seCheck
tab[, c("n", "simMean", "theoMean", "simSD", "theoSE", "seRatio", "seOK")]
```

```{r}
#| label: sePlot
plotSE(tab, label = "Exponential")
```

Center: the simulated mean was slightly below mu = 1 at `r sum(tab$simMean < 1)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes. Measured in Monte Carlo standard errors
(theoretical SE / sqrt(num)), the gap was above 2 at `r sum(meanGapZ > 2)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes, with a largest value of
`r round(max(meanGapZ), 2)`. At first this looked like a problem, but it comes from my seed design: because I reset the seed
before each n, the run for sample size n uses the first n × num random numbers of the same stream. The rows share
most of their random numbers, so if the stream happens to run a little low, every row moves down together. These are
not `r nrow(tab)` independent checks of the mean, and a gap under 3 standard errors from one stream is not unusual.

Spread: the SE ratio stayed between `r round(seRange[1], 3)` and `r round(seRange[2], 3)` at every n, including n = 1, and
`r sum(tab$seOK)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes passed my 5 percent SE check. The formula sigma / sqrt(n) does not need a large n;
it holds for any n because it only uses independence and a finite variance.

# 6. Why did you choose that value?

```{r}
#| label: samplingPlots
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 6
plotSampling(res, nShow = unique(c(5, 30, nStar, 500)), mu = pop$mu, theoSE = iidSE(pop$sigma), label = pop$label)
```

At n = 5 the histogram is clearly right skewed and the QQ plot bends upward at the right end. At n = 30 the bend is
smaller but still visible: the right tail of the QQ plot sits above the line and the left tail sits above it too,
which is the shape of a distribution with a short left tail and a long right tail. At n = `r nStar` a small bend is still
visible at the lower end, but much less than at n = 30. At n = 500 the points follow the line.

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4
plotConvergence(tab, label = "Exponential")
```

The simulated skewness follows the red prediction 2 / sqrt(n) closely and crosses my cutoff near n = 100.

Is n = 30 enough? If the sampling distribution were normal, 2.5 percent of the standardized means would fall in
each tail beyond ±1.96. At n = 30 the lower tail held `r round(100 * at30$tailLow, 2)` percent and the upper tail held
`r round(100 * at30$tailHigh, 2)` percent. So a 95 percent interval built from the normal approximation at n = 30 would land entirely above the true mean about
`r round(at30$tailHigh / at30$tailLow, 1)` times as often as entirely below it, instead of equally often.

I chose n = `r nStar` because:

* At n = `r nStar` the skewness was `r round(star$skew, 3)`, the excess kurtosis `r round(star$exKurt, 3)` and the QQ correlation
  `r round(star$qqCor, 4)`, all within my cutoffs, and every larger n I tested also passed.
* At the largest n that still failed (n = `r lastFail$n`), the check that failed was `r paste(names(failed)[failed], collapse = " and ")`
  (skewness `r round(lastFail$skew, 3)`).
* The result matches the prediction from section 2, which I made before running the simulation.

# 7. What surprised you?

```{r}
#| label: predictionCheck
predictionCheck <- data.frame(
  Prediction = c(
    "Mean of the sample means equals 1 at every n (within noise)",
    "SE equals 1 / sqrt(n) at every n, including n = 1",
    "Right skewed at small n, QQ plot bends up at both ends",
    paste("Skewness about 2 / sqrt(30) =", round(2 / sqrt(30), 3), "at n = 30, so n = 30 is not enough"),
    "Skewness, not kurtosis, decides the answer",
    paste("Smallest normal n is about", predictedN(pop$gamma1)),
    "(Assumed, not written in section 2) Once n passes, larger n also pass",
    "Shapiro Wilk rejects at almost every n"
  ),
  Result = c(
    paste0("Below 1 at ", sum(tab$simMean < 1), " of ", nrow(tab), " n; gap above 2 Monte Carlo SEs at ", sum(meanGapZ > 2), " n"),
    paste0("SE ratio ", round(seRange[1], 3), " to ", round(seRange[2], 3), "; ", sum(tab$seOK), " of ", nrow(tab), " passed"),
    "Seen at n = 5 and n = 30 (section 6)",
    paste0("Skewness ", round(at30$skew, 3), "; tails ", round(100 * at30$tailLow, 2), "% and ", round(100 * at30$tailHigh, 2), "%"),
    paste0("Last failure (n = ", lastFail$n, ") failed on ", paste(names(failed)[failed], collapse = " and ")),
    paste("n =", nStar),
    paste0("n = ", paste(lucky, collapse = " and "), " passed, then larger n failed again"),
    paste0("Rejected at ", sum(tab$swP < 0.05), " of ", nrow(tab), " n")
  ),
  Match = c("Different", "Same", "Same", "Same", "Same", "Same", "Different", "Same")
)
knitr::kable(predictionCheck)
```

I split the four predictions from section 2 into seven statements I could check. Six of them held, and one thing I had assumed without writing it down did not. The formula 2 / sqrt(n) predicted both the size of the skewness at n = 30
(`r round(2 / sqrt(30), 3)` predicted, `r round(at30$skew, 3)` simulated) and the final answer (`r predictedN(pop$gamma1)` predicted,
`r nStar` simulated). Two results were different from what I expected.

The mean. I expected the simulated mean to scatter around 1, sometimes above and sometimes below. Instead it was
below 1 at `r sum(tab$simMean < 1)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes, and more than 2 Monte Carlo standard errors below at `r sum(meanGapZ > 2)` of them.
This is not a problem with the CLT; it comes from resetting the seed before every n. The run for sample size n
uses the first n × num random numbers of one stream, so the rows share most of their random numbers and move
together (section 5). I had been treating the rows as independent checks, and they are not.

The order of passing. I assumed that once a sample size passed, the larger ones would pass too. Near the cutoff
that was not true: n = `r paste(lucky, collapse = " and ")` passed while n values right after them failed. Near n = 100 the true
skewness is less than one noise band away from the cutoff, so whether a single row passes is partly luck. This is why my rule requires
every larger n to pass, not just the first one that does.

## Limitations

* My answer of n = `r nStar` belongs to my cutoffs. With a skewness cutoff of 0.1 the same population needed
  n = `r skewCompare$chosenN[skewCompare$skewCut == 0.1]`, so the number should always be reported together with the standard behind it.
* The exact boundary is uncertain by a few n, because the predicted skewness crosses the cutoff right at 100 and
  the noise band is about ±`r round(band, 3)` wide. A different seed could give a slightly different answer; I test this in
  the reproducibility file.
* I only simulated lambda = 1. Section 2 showed that lambda does not change the shape, so this does not limit the
  conclusion for exponential populations, but it says nothing about other skewed populations.
* All rows come from one random stream (seed `r student_id`), so they are not independent of each other.
